summary: The developer can start building the Node.js LlamaIndex + Azure DocumentDB sample now: the local machine has Node/npx, the DocumentDB MCP server, the Microsoft Learn search server, Azure CLI signed-in, and the set of DocumentDB agent skills installed. Important factual confusions were found in the cold answers (many are old Cosmos DB or other-product assumptions) but each has authoritative Microsoft Learn pages to correct them. Missing tools (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) are non-blocking for the sample; mongosh would speed manual checks. The build can proceed with workarounds and a few clarifications (LLM selection, seed-data shape, embedding dimension decisions).
summary_points: Build can start: Node.js (v24), npx, the 'documentdb' MCP server, the 'learn' Docs MCP server and Azure CLI are available and sufficient to implement, inspect and verify the sample against the live cluster.

Many cold answers were confused with Cosmos DB (RU model) or Amazon DocumentDB; authoritative docs show the correct resource types (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters), CLI group (az documentdb), vCore billing model, integrated vector & text search, and mongo+OIDC connection strings.

No MCP server or skill the sample critically depends on is missing, but developer conveniences are absent: mongosh, azd, bicep and terraform are not on PATH; mongosh is worth adding to speed manual verification.

Information gaps remain around LLM provider / model choices, embedding dimension selection and a canonical sample document shape — these are not answered by the installed skills or the Learn docs searched here.
Verdict is ready_with_gaps: the build proceeds, but follow the guidance corrections below and add a small seed script and README to avoid ambiguous choices during the implementation.

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run the Node.js sample, install npm packages, run LlamaIndex integration and sample scripts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or build the Node.js LlamaIndex agent or sample code.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js 24 (or compatible LTS) prior to build. The sample must run on Node 24 as specified in the prompt.

tools.name: npx
tools.needed_for: Install and run MCP-related tools and any dev-time scripts; typical Node tool invocations and skill installation helpers.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to run one-off scripts or npx-scoped tools; developer would need to install global packages instead.
tools.workaround: Install npm / npx via Node installer or use npm script alternatives.

tools.name: npm (implied via Node/npx)
tools.needed_for: Install project dependencies (mongodb driver, llamaindex client, OpenAI/Azure OpenAI SDKs).

tools.name: az
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources, read cluster resources if needed (e.g., firewall rules, private endpoint configuration), and run control-plane checks.
tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1, signed in (Visual Studio Enterprise Subscription)
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot inspect resource group or cluster control-plane; would limit ability to confirm networking or to create optional firewall rules.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal to inspect settings; the sample's run-environment already exposes DOCUMENTDB_URI so control-plane writes are not required.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the DocumentDB local gateway container for local dev / tests.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run a local DocumentDB gateway; must use the live reachable cluster instead (which is already the intended behaviour).
tools.workaround: Build and verify against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as the prompt instructs.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane checks: list databases, examine collections/indexes, sample documents, explain query plans, create indexes and verify the sample created collections and indexes.
tools.detail: Available with 18 data-plane tools (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_create_index, etc.). Every call must pass connection_profile "default".
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to programmatically verify collections, indexes and query plans from the build environment; manual checks would be required.
tools.workaround: Use the Node.js driver to inspect collections and indexes directly; use the Azure portal for some control-plane information.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative documentation search and grounding for ambiguous or conflicting cold answers.
tools.detail: learn_microsoft_docs_search and docs fetch tools available.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to find authoritative Microsoft guidance quickly; increased risk of relying on stale memory.
tools.workaround: Use web search manually or local docs; but for reproducible agent behaviour prefer the Learn MCP server.

tools.name: azure (Azure MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Control-plane best-practices, Azure CLI command generation, and other Azure guidance if IaC is added.
tools.detail: Available; many azure_* tools (azure_documentation, azure_azd, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Less convenient generation of accurate Azure CLI commands and best-practice checks.
tools.workaround: Manually derive needed CLI commands or use learn docs.

tools.name: installed DocumentDB agent skills (documentdb-driver, documentdb-connection, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-data-modeling, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-mcp-setup, documentdb-security, documentdb-natural-language-querying)
tools.needed_for: Design guidance, connection best practices, indexing/vector-search recipes, security guidance, local dev tips, and query-generation helpers for DocumentDB-specific behaviour.
tools.detail: Multiple DocumentDB-specific skills are installed (see inventory list).
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lack curated, product-specific guidance for driver instantiation, vector indexes, and connection patterns; greater chance of mistakes.
tools.workaround: Rely on general MongoDB driver docs and Microsoft Learn pages, but expect more effort and potential for subtle mistakes.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual connectivity tests, ad-hoc queries, and developer sanity-checks against the cluster (useful during development to quickly inspect collections and run $search queries).
tools.impact_if_missing: No direct shell for manual, interactive checks; developers must use the Node driver or the documentdb MCP server for ad-hoc queries.
tools.workaround: Use documentdb MCP server tools to sample docs and run queries programmatically, or use Node-based scripts for ad-hoc queries; install mongosh to speed manual checks.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (for the account/cluster).
confusions.grounded_answer: The resource provider namespace is Microsoft.DocumentDB and the current resource type for a managed Azure DocumentDB cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflects the older Cosmos DB resource model (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) used by Cosmos DB accounts; the new managed MongoDB-compatible offering uses a dedicated mongoClusters resource type under the same provider namespace.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) ARM / Bicep docs (example)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder tried to create or refer to Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in IaC for this new service, the deployment would target the wrong resource type and fail or create a different product (Cosmos DB account).
improvements: Update quickstart and resource docs to show the new recommended resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters prominently on the 'create cluster' and 'quickstart' pages.
Add a deprecation note on any page that still recommends Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for vCore clusters, pointing to the mongoClusters resource.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct control-plane CLI group for Azure DocumentDB clusters is az documentdb (subgroup mongocluster), e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create ... — not az cosmosdb.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both products are in the Microsoft.DocumentDB namespace historically and many Cosmos DB examples used az cosmosdb; the cold answer came from older Cosmos DB CLI habits.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands would operate on the Cosmos DB control plane (databaseAccounts) rather than the DocumentDB mongoClusters. This would mis-provision resources or fail to find the existing mongoClusters.
improvements: In CLI quickstarts and agent-kit README, clearly show az documentdb mongocluster commands for DocumentDB and add a short sentence: 'Do not use az cosmosdb for this product; use az documentdb.'
Add an example az documentdb mongocluster create snippet on the top of the 'create cluster' doc.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep / ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep / ARM and Terraform should use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (learn templates show microsoft.documentdb/mongoclusters). Terraform examples use the AzAPI provider or the mongoClusters resource types / AVM modules that target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters rather than azurerm_cosmosdb_account for this product.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both older Cosmos DB workflows and some migration documents mention Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and azurerm_cosmosdb_account; the new vCore offering uses a dedicated 'mongoClusters' resource which looks different in IaC.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong resource type in IaC would create the wrong service (Cosmos DB account) or fail to create a DocumentDB mongoClusters resource; the sample's instruction is to use an existing cluster so this is more about accurate docs and optional IaC.
improvements: Add a short 'IaC' section on the DocumentDB quickstart pages with Bicep and Terraform snippets that show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and link to the AVM module for mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-style connection string for Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB for MongoDB API): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<account>@. If using SRV: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Username is typically in the form <dbuser>@<account>. Port for TLS is 10255. Required options: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false (recommended for Cosmos), and appName or maxIdleTimeMS as recommended by driver docs.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB clusters use the mongodb+srv scheme for best behaviour (host <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com), TLS must be enabled (tls=true), and recommended options include authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID auth or SCRAM auth for native users, retryWrites=false and maxIdleTimeMS as best-practice. The older Cosmos DB 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com' + port 10255 style is not the correct modern endpoint for this service. For local DocumentDB gateways the development gateway uses port 10260 (and tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (azure-portal)
Quickstart: Connect using MongoDB Shell (Learn)
Development loop — DocumentDB local gateway (Learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed older Cosmos DB-for-MongoDB endpoints (mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255) with the newer DocumentDB cluster hostnames and the local gateway conventions. Both share 'cosmos' and 'mongo' tokens which cause easy mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB MongoDB API connection strings and older docs

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host/port or options could cause connection failures (ECONNREFUSED or TLS errors) or incorrect auth method (expecting SCRAM vs OIDC). The agent must use the connection string format provided by the cluster's Connection strings UI and prefer mongodb+srv when directed.
improvements: Document the recommended SRV-style connection string and examples for both native (SCRAM) and Microsoft Entra ID (MONGODB-OIDC) authentication on the quickstart page.
Add a single 'connection string' example block to the sample prompt and README showing use of DOCUMENTDB_URI and the expected scheme (mongodb+srv) and options.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) is billed as provisioned throughput measured in Request Units (RU/s) or by serverless consumption; you provision RU/s at database/container level (with autoscale available) or use serverless option. There is not a vCore-based billing model for the classic Cosmos DB Mongo API (billing is RU-based or serverless).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the managed MongoDB-compatible vCore offering) is billed by compute tiers (vCores) and storage (the M-series tiers like M30, M40 etc.), not by Request Units. The vCore + storage model is the correct model for this product (the RU model applies to Azure Cosmos DB's RU-based offering, which is a different service).

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Compute and storage configurations for Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the RU-based Cosmos DB pricing model; Azure DocumentDB intentionally chose a vCore compute-tier model and was formerly described as 'vCore-based Cosmos DB for MongoDB'. The shared naming and overlap in namespaces caused the mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB request units docs (RU model)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RU-based autoscale and tried to tune or measure RUs, they would choose the wrong scaling knobs and incorrect cost model; provisioning guidance and cluster sizing would be wrong.
improvements: Add a clear comparison box at the top of the DocumentDB 'pricing' and 'overview' pages explicitly stating: 'This product uses vCore+storage billing; do not confuse with Cosmos DB RU model.'
Add sample cost-estimate guidance for typical M30/M40 choices next to the quickstart for common migration scenarios.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Data-plane authentication for the MongoDB API is typically username/password (SCRAM) using the account/database user credentials (or the account primary key encoded into a MongoDB user). Management plane uses Azure AD. Direct MongoDB driver authentication via Microsoft Entra ID is not generally supported for the MongoDB wire protocol; to use Azure AD you must use the Azure management SDKs or features that explicitly support Azure AD. So in-app drivers: use the MongoDB connection string with username/password (SCRAM) and tls/ssl options.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native username/password authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for data-plane authentication. Drivers can authenticate using Microsoft Entra ID via the MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC) or via password-based native users; the docs show how to obtain connection strings for both modes (and recommend SRV + tls=true when appropriate).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (azure-portal)
Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically some Cosmos DB APIs didn't support AD for data-plane; the cold answer assumed that limitation and did not reflect the DocumentDB MONGODB-OIDC support shown in current docs.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only SCRAM and ignores OIDC support, they might implement a password-based flow where an organization wanted OIDC-managed credentials (managed identity) — that changes secret handling and deployment steps.
improvements: Add an example in the quickstart showing both SCRAM and MONGODB-OIDC connection string templates and the small steps necessary to enable Microsoft Entra ID on the cluster UI.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For application data access use a standard MongoDB driver (for Node.js: the official mongodb npm package). There is no separate data-plane SDK specific to Cosmos Mongo API for application reads/writes — use the MongoDB driver and the connection string. For management/administration use the Azure SDK (az cosmosdb commands or @azure/arm-cosmosdb).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the official MongoDB drivers (Node.js: mongodb npm package) for data-plane access. Management tasks (control plane) use Azure CLI / ARM/az APIs.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: If vector indexes are available on the cluster they follow vector engines such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. The creation is done with a MongoDB createIndex-style command on the collection. Example (approximate): db.segments.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_vector_hnsw', engine: 'hnsw', 'vector.dim': 1536, 'vector.metric': 'cosine' }) — (driver call: db.collection('segments').createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { engine: 'hnsw', 'vector.dim': 1536, 'vector.metric': 'cosine' })). Note: exact option names vary; treat engine:'hnsw' / 'ivf' / 'diskann' and vector.dim / vector.metric as the expected parameters.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports IVF, HNSW and DiskANN vector index kinds and uses a createIndexes/runCommand JSON template with a cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions block (not the community MongoDB engine:key/value pair used in the cold example). Example pattern uses a createIndexes runCommand with cosmosSearchOptions.kind set to 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' and options such as 'dimensions', 'similarity', and engine-specific tuning fields (m, efConstruction, numLists, lBuild, maxDegree etc.). Searches use the $search aggregation stage with the cosmosSearch operator.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Quickstart: Use vector search with Node.js

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed a MongoDB engine-style index creation syntax (engine:'hnsw') from some vector-extended MongoDB servers; Azure DocumentDB implements vector indexes through its own createIndexes/runCommand with cosmosSearchOptions JSON and different option names.

confusion_sources.title: Community example for vector indexes on other platforms (Atlas)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong createIndex syntax will fail to create a usable vector index or will create a nonfunctional index; the sample that uses embeddings and vector search would not work.
improvements: Add a short code snippet showing the exact createIndexes JSON for HNSW/IVF/DiskANN on the vector-search quickstart page (the docs already do this in detail; ensure it's prominent).

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text and hybrid (vector + text) search is not provided through the MongoDB wire protocol itself on classic Cosmos DB; you use Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) connected to Cosmos DB (indexer or push indexing) to get full-text and hybrid search. If the managed service exposes an integrated search engine (like Atlas Search), you would use its API; otherwise wire up Azure Cognitive Search and optionally augment it with vectors stored separately or indexed via the search service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect: Azure DocumentDB includes integrated full-text and vector search with createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch operator). Hybrid scenarios (lexical BM25 + vector) and text- and vector-indexing are supported natively; you don't have to route through Azure Cognitive Search for typical full-text or hybrid vector+text use cases.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Full-text and hybrid search with createSearchIndexes and $search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB users used Azure Cognitive Search for full-text scenarios; the new DocumentDB offering integrates text and vector search directly and uses different operator names (cosmosSearch) which the cold answer overlooked.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder wired the sample to Azure Cognitive Search assuming DocumentDB lacks native search, they would add unnecessary complexity and cost and might mismatch query syntax.
improvements: Make the integrated text+vector search examples very prominent on the product overview and quickstart pages (including hybrid BM25+vector examples).

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB API exposes compatibility modes based on MongoDB server versions (commonly 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 5.0 and newer in newer accounts). Newer clusters may support MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol depending on the account configuration. However some MongoDB server features are limited or different: server-side JavaScript (db.eval) and some server extensions are not supported; multi-document transactions and certain aggregation stages or change-stream behaviour can be limited depending on the API version. Expect behavioural differences in indexing, geospatial edge cases and transaction semantics versus a native MongoDB server.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and provides 99.03% operator coverage; a detailed compatibility reference is available. Many common MongoDB features are supported; administrative commands and some low-level server-side admin operations are restricted by the PaaS model. The exact unsupported operators are itemised in the MongoDB compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance — MongoDB compatibility
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged and mixed older Cosmos compatibility statements with the newer DocumentDB compatibility guarantees; the authoritative docs list supported wire versions and the feature-coverage tables.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed an older or narrower wire-protocol support, they might pick an incompatible driver or miss newer aggregation features available on the cluster.
improvements: Add a compact 'supported wire versions' box to the quickstart and compatibility pages so agents find it easily.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: For local development run a MongoDB Docker container (official MongoDB image) and point your app at localhost:27017. Example: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo mongo:7 --bind_ip_all. There is also the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for SQL/Graph/Table/Cassandra APIs, but it has limited or no support for the MongoDB API; therefore prefer a local MongoDB image for Mongo-protocol development.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the DocumentDB local gateway Docker image for local development (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) which exposes the DocumentDB gateway on port 10260 and expects TLS; the quickstart shows docker run ... -p 10260:10260 and a connection string like mongodb://<admin>:<password>@localhost:10260/?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true. The official MongoDB image is not the recommended local emulator for this product.

grounding_links.title: Development loop — DocumentDB local gateway

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed generic MongoDB local development practices instead of the product-specific DocumentDB local gateway that the DocumentDB quickstart documents.

confusion_sources.title: Docker run official MongoDB local image docs (community)

confusions.build_risk: Using a plain MongoDB container for local tests may lead to differences in features (e.g., DocumentDB-specific vector and search behaviours) and mislead the developer about service behaviour; the prompt explicitly preferred the live cluster, but the local gateway recipe is available if needed.
improvements: Make the local gateway example highly visible in the quickstart and the sample templates so developers don't default to the generic Mongo image.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: The MongoDB changeStreams API is not universally supported on Cosmos DB's MongoDB API historically. Cosmos DB provides its own Change Feed feature which is the recommended way to consume data changes. If you need MongoDB-style change streams, verify the account's MongoDB wire version and feature support; otherwise use the Cosmos DB change feed (enabled by default at the container level).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style change streams. For some multishard scenarios or preview features you may need to enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' preview feature in cluster settings; Mongoose Model.watch() maps to the DocumentDB change-streams capability per the docs. The product docs explain nuances around enabling change streams for multishard clusters.

grounding_links.title: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB: Model.watch() and change streams
Change streams (Learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB accounts and some API versions did not expose MongoDB change streams; the cold answer reflected that historical limitation rather than current DocumentDB capabilities.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unavailable they might implement a polling-based approach or use a different change-capture mechanism — both add complexity and latency.
improvements: Clarify the steps to enable change streams for multishard clusters in a short 'enable change streams' note in the quickstart.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (named 'documentdb' in the environment). The general Azure MCP server handles management-plane Azure operations, but the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane inspection tools (collections, indexes, query plans) specific to the Mongo-compatible DocumentDB service. Example: mcp documentdb --profile default inspect-collection sample_retail_08.segments
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides the data-plane tools for collection/index/query inspection; the azure MCP server is for control-plane tasks. The inventory shows a documentdb MCP server with the expected data-plane tools.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically 'DocumentDB' was Microsoft Azure's original JSON document database service and the prefix for what became Azure Cosmos DB. Azure DocumentDB merged into/was renamed to Azure Cosmos DB; Cosmos DB provides multiple APIs (SQL, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table). This service (MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB) is the MongoDB API endpoint of Cosmos DB (or a managed Mongo-compatible offering) and is separate from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly incorrect: The historical 'DocumentDB' (2014) did become Azure Cosmos DB, but the current product 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' is the vCore-based offering that was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and is now a distinct product that runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine. Azure DocumentDB (vCore) and Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) are separate services and the new name clarifies that split.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? — naming and history
Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical renames: (1) the original Azure DocumentDB (2014) evolved into Cosmos DB, (2) the vCore-based Cosmos DB for MongoDB offering was later renamed 'Azure DocumentDB'. The cold answer conflated these historic name-changes.
confusions.build_risk: Documentation or sample text that uses the wrong product name (Cosmos DB vs Azure DocumentDB vs DocumentDB) will confuse readers and may lead to use of the wrong service APIs.
improvements: Add a single FAQ paragraph near the product name that succinctly explains the lineage and the deliberate naming difference between 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore)' and 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)'.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API, the underlying engine is the Azure Cosmos DB engine (a different implementation than upstream MongoDB) that speaks the MongoDB wire protocol. That means application code using MongoDB drivers generally works, but you may encounter differences in supported features, transaction semantics, indexing behaviour, query planner differences, and some unsupported commands. Use the MongoDB driver for normal reads/writes, but test critical features against the target cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation), not the Cosmos DB engine; it speaks the MongoDB wire protocol so MongoDB drivers work but there are product-specific differences (administrative commands, some unsupported operators). Applications generally use standard MongoDB drivers unchanged, but test compatibility and use the migration compatibility assessment for edge cases.

grounding_links.title: What is DocumentDB (in Azure) — Implementations
Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the product was a rebrand of Cosmos DB's internal engine; in fact the product is built on the open-source DocumentDB project and differs from Cosmos DB's RU model and engine.
confusions.build_risk: If the developer assumes the Cosmos DB engine they may expect RU semantics or other control-plane behaviours that don't apply; this mostly affects IaC and billing assumptions rather than application-level CRUD code.
improvements: Document that Azure DocumentDB runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine and call out the practical consequences for billing and admin commands.

confusions.question: What connection string environment variable and runtime behaviour will this sample rely on?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the MongoDB connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. The sample will not persist this secret; it will only be read from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and passed to the Node.js mongodb driver. Example usage in code: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; const client = new MongoClient(uri, { tls: true, retryWrites: false });
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the sample runtime should read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI. Use the connection string template provided by the cluster's Connection strings UI and do not commit secrets to source control. Use TLS/tls=true in driver options and set retryWrites=false as recommended when appropriate.

grounding_links.title: Skill run-environment (sample prompt)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (Learn)

confusions.question: Which database and collections will the sample create and use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_retail_08. Create two collections: segments (stores customer segment documents with a purchase history and embedding vector) and campaigns (stores generated campaign drafts). Example creation calls: db.getSiblingDB('sample_retail_08').createCollection('segments'); db.sample_retail_08.createCollection('campaigns');
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct as an implementation decision: the prompt's skill_md explicitly requests the sample use database sample_retail_08 and a 'campaigns' collection; collection names are not rigidly specified by platform docs and the builder's choice of 'segments' and 'campaigns' is reasonable.

confusions.question: Which Node.js client and exact connect code will the sample use to fetch segments?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official mongodb npm package. Example connection code to run at startup: const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb'); const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; const client = new MongoClient(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true, retryWrites: false }); await client.connect(); const db = client.db('sample_retail_08'); const segments = db.collection('segments'); // then segments.find({ ... })
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct approach: use the official mongodb npm driver, and use a process-level singleton MongoClient per documentdb-driver guidance. The driver options should include TLS and recommended options; the exact driver options (useNewUrlParser/useUnifiedTopology) vary by driver major-version, so follow the latest driver docs for Node 24 and mongodb driver v5+ patterns.

confusions.question: What index(es) does this sample need for vector search and the lookup patterns?
confusions.cold_answer: Create an index on the embedding field for vector search using the cluster's vector engine and a standard index on segment id and customer id for fast lookups. Example (approximate): db.segments.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_hnsw', engine: 'hnsw', 'vector.dim': 1536, 'vector.metric': 'cosine' }); db.segments.createIndex({ segmentId: 1 }); db.campaigns.createIndex({ campaignId: 1 });
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct: the sample should create a standard single-field index on the lookup keys (segmentId or name) and, if vector search is used, create a vector index using the DocumentDB createIndexes JSON format with cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' and dimensions/similarity. The exact createIndexes command syntax differs from a naive createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, ...).

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a generic MongoDB engine-style vector index creation API; DocumentDB exposes vector indexing through its createIndexes/runCommand JSON schema and cosmosSearchOptions fields.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses incorrect createIndex syntax, vector indexes won't be created and vector search will fail. Lookup indexes (segmentId) are straightforward and should be created exactly as named.
improvements: Add a ready-to-copy createIndexes JSON example for the sample 'segments' collection (HNSW with dimensions matching chosen embedding model) into the sample README.

confusions.question: What MCP/documentdb commands will be used to inspect collections, indexes and query plans as part of verification?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile 'default' to inspect collections and indexes. Example commands (approximate): mcp documentdb --profile default list-collections sample_retail_08 mcp documentdb --profile default show-indexes sample_retail_08.segments mcp documentdb --profile default explain-query "db.segments.find({...}).limit(10)". If mcp has explicit verbs: mcp documentdb inspect-collection --profile default sample_retail_08.segments and mcp documentdb explain --profile default "{ find: 'segments', filter: {...} }".
confusions.grounded_answer: The environment includes a documentdb MCP server with tools such as documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_get_statistics and documentdb_explain_operation. Use these documented MCP server tools (pass connection_profile 'default') to list databases/collections, list indexes and run explain/explainOperation for queries. The exact verbs in the local mcp CLI depend on the MCP client wrapper, but the installed MCP tools match the named functions available in the inventory.
